nodes.name: One-pot Hydrothermal Synthesis and Calcination
nodes.procedure: The Ni-doped RuO₂ sample was prepared using a one-pot hydrothermal method followed by calcination in air, as illustrated in Figure 2a and Figure S4.
nodes.source_text: Based on the DFT calculations, the Ni-doped RuO₂ sample was prepared using a one-pot hydrothermal method followed by calcination in air, as illustrated in Figure 2a and Figure S4.

nodes.description: HER performance in 1 M KOH using three-electrode RDE setup
nodes.source_text: The HER catalytic activities of as-prepared electrocatalysts were evaluated by linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves. The LSV curves indicate that the Ni-RuO₂ catalyst demonstrates the most efficient HER catalytic activity... Ni-RuO₂ achieves the lowest overpotential of 9mV at 10mAcm⁻²... overpotential of 42mV even at 100mAcm⁻²... low overpotential of 134mV at a high current density of 1000mAcm⁻²... much smaller Tafel slope (20.85mVdec⁻¹)... exchange current density 4.16mA cm⁻²... TOF values of Ni-RuO₂ are 7.42H₂s⁻¹... mass activity of 40.1A mg_meta⁻¹... chronoamperometry tests reveal that Ni-RuO₂ catalyst maintains its potential without significant change over 180 hours

nodes.description: Double layer capacitance and ECSA measurement
nodes.source_text: Double layer capacitances (C_dl) of the samples were performed to obtain the electrochemically active surface area (ECSA)... The higher C_dl of Ni-RuO₂ suggests a larger ECSA for electrocatalysis

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni-RuO2 and RuO2 exhibit XRD patterns consistent with standard RuO2 (PDF: 71-2273), with (110) peak at 2θ=28.1° shifting to lower angles for Ni-RuO2.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Both the RuO2 and Ni-RuO2 samples exhibit similar XRD patterns, and all peaks are well-consistent with standard RuO2 (PDF: 71-2273) (Figure S5a). The main peak, (110) at 2θ = 28.1°, reveals a shift to lower angles (Figure S5b)

properties.description: Tafel plot showing overpotential (η) vs log current density

nodes.characterization_summary: RuO2 nanoparticles have average diameter of 2.7 nm; Ni-RuO2 shows similar morphology with lattice fringe distance of 0.32 nm matching (110) planes of RuO2 and visible defect sites.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (Figure S7a) reveals that the un-doped RuO2 has a nanoparticle morphology with an average diameter of 2.7 nm ... The Ni-RuO2 (Figure S7c) sample exhibits a morphology similar to that of undoped RuO2

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni-RuO2 shows interplanar distance of 0.32 nm for (110) crystal face with obvious defect sites; after reduction at -0.005 V vs RHE, additional 0.24 nm spacing for Ru (100) planes with intertwined lattice-misaligned interface.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Its high-resolution TEM image displays an interplanar distance of 0.32 nm related to the (110) crystal face (Figure 2b), and obvious defect sites are highlighted in yellow circles ... High-resolution TEM (HRTEM) characterization of Ni-RuO2 sample reduced at -0.005 V reveals two different interplanar spacings (Figure 3f)

properties.description: High-resolution TEM image with lattice fringes

nodes.characterization_summary: EDX elemental mapping shows homogeneous distribution of elements in Ni-RuO2.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) spectroscopy demonstrates that elements distribute homogeneously in Ni-RuO2 (Figure 2c)

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni-RuO2 Ni 2p peaks at 856.2 eV (2p3/2), 873.8 eV (2p1/2) indicate Ni2+; Ru 3d5/2 shifts from 280.7 eV (RuO2) to 280.9 eV; O1s -OH increases from 33.83% (RuO2) to 37.32% (Ni-RuO2) confirming oxygen vacancies.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The Ni 2p XPS spectrum (Figure S8b) exhibits two primary peaks at 856.2 and 873.8 eV ... The percentage of -OH increases from 33.83% for RuO2 to 37.32% for Ni-RuO2, confirming that the presence of Ni2+ introduces additional Ov sites

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni K-edge XANES of Ni-RuO2 shows absorption profile nearly identical to NiO, confirming average Ni oxidation state of +2.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The Ni K-edge X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) spectra for Ni atoms in RuO2 alongside reference spectra for Ni foil and NiO are displayed in Figure 2d. The Ni K-edge absorption profile of the Ni-RuO2 shows almost the same energy compared to NiO

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni K-edge EXAFS of Ni-RuO2 shows single peak at ~1.52 Å for Ni-O coordination within RuO2 lattice, no Ni-Ni peak observed unlike Ni foil.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In the reference NiO, two primary peaks are observed at around 2.54 and 1.55 Å, aligned with Ni-Ni and Ni-O coordination, respectively (Figure 2e). In contrast, the Ni-RuO2 sample shows a single peak at ∼1.52 Å, attributed to Ni-O coordination within the RuO2 lattice

properties.description: Radial distribution function from Ni foil

nodes.characterization_summary: CV of Ni-RuO2 shows H adsorption/desorption peaks at -0.005 V vs RHE vs -0.1 V for RuO2, confirming Ni2+ triggers RuO2→Ru reduction at 20x lower overpotential.
nodes.evidence_snippet: for the Ni-RuO2 sample, the hydrogen adsorption and desorption peaks appear in samples reduced at low potentials (-0.005 V vs. RHE Figure 3b) ... the activation overpotentials for Ni-RuO2 and RuO2 are determined as being -0.005 and -0.1 V, respectively, with the introduction of Ni2+ providing at least 20 times energy savings

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni-RuO2 shows higher Cdl than RuO2, indicating larger ECSA due to increased surface defects from Ni2+ doping.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Double layer capacitances (Cdl) of the samples were performed to obtain the electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) (Figure S11). The higher Cdl of Ni-RuO2 suggests a larger ECSA for electrocatalysis

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni-RuO2 shows charge transfer resistance Rct of 1.21 Ω, significantly lower than Ru/C (5.25 Ω), Pt/C (3.06 Ω), and commercial RuO2 (5.08 Ω).
nodes.evidence_snippet: Figure S12b presents the electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS) of these catalysts. The charge transfer resistance (Rct) value of Ni-RuO2 is fitted to be 1.21Ω which is significantly smaller than that of the Ru/C (5.25Ω) Pt/C (3.06Ω) and commercial RuO2 (5.08Ω)
